                  REPLY BRIEF OF COMMISSION TRIAL STAFF

        Pursuant to the order establishing paper hearing procedures issued by the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) in this proceeding, 1 Commission Trial

Staff (Trial Staff) submits its reply brief in response to the initial brief filed by New

England Transmission Owners (NETOs) on August 28, 2026. 2

        This proceeding concerns a proposal by the Participating Transmission Owners

Administrative Committee (PTO AC) to increase the base rate of return on equity (ROE)

set forth in the Open Access Transmission Tariff of ISO New England Inc.

Accompanying this brief is a reply affidavit of Robert J. Keyton, in which Mr. Keyton

responds to certain points in the initial filings of NETOs and other parties. 3 As discussed

below, NETOs fail to demonstrate that the proposed base ROE of 11.39 percent is just

and reasonable. The proposal should therefore be rejected.

                                       ARGUMENT

       In multiple respects, NETOs are attempting to have it both ways. They insist that

this proceeding is narrowly confined to application of Commission ROE policy, yet they

go out of their way to criticize that policy and rely on the testimony of a consultant who

does the same. They assert that PTO AC’s filing simply updates market data to reflect

contemporary conditions, yet they preemptively criticize any recommendation that would

refine the policy to similarly reflect these changed conditions. And they repeatedly claim

that the initial testimony of Adrien McKenzie faithfully and precisely applies

Commission policy, but then in the next breath they essentially ask the Commission to

accept a significant correction to this same purportedly precise application of policy.

       Contrary to NETOs’ suggestion, the development of an ROE is not a plug-and-

play process. If it were, NETOs presumably would not have retained the services of an

outside consultant and a team of at least 11 outside attorneys from four different law

firms. In doing so, NETOs implicitly recognize that the discounted cash flow (DCF)

analysis and capital asset pricing model (CAPM) are complex frameworks requiring

numerous judgment calls.

       Perhaps this is most apparent in the selection of a proxy group. As discussed

below, NETOs fail to justify several of PTO AC’s decisions with respect to the proxy

group composition. The erroneous exclusion of Eversource Energy (Eversource) – this

proceeding’s namesake – is particularly notable, as the mergers and acquisitions (M&A)

activity of Eversource does not come close to meeting the standard for exclusion.



                                             2
           NETOs also offer no credible justification for other departures from Commission

policy. Among these is PTO AC’s use of Value Line betas for the CAPM analysis when

Bloomberg betas are in the record. Precedent is clear that Bloomberg betas are to be

applied under these circumstances.

A.        Neither the Scope of the Hearing nor the Contents of PTO AC’s Filing Are as
          Narrow as NETOs Claim

          NETOs assert that the Commission narrowly confined the scope of this proceeding

to PTO AC’s application of the Commission’s revised ROE methodology, and they claim

that PTO AC’s filing did not advocate for changes to this policy. 4 NETOs are incorrect

on both counts.

          The Commission set for paper hearing procedures “PTO AC’s proposed ROE.” 5

While the Commission did specify that these procedures “should address” the PTO AC’s

application of the Commission’s revised ROE methodology, the Commission did not in

any way indicate that the hearing was to be limited only to addressing this aspect of the

proposal. 6 Accordingly, to the extent the participants have recommended refinements to

current policy as appropriate for analyzing the justness and reasonableness of PTO AC’s

proposed ROE, such recommendations are properly before the Commission.

          For example, Mr. Keyton suggested in his initial affidavit that the Commission

reconsider the weighting of the short- and long-term growth rates in the DCF model, as

          It is rather ironic that NETOs attempt to preempt any arguments that “revisit

policy and methodological issues already resolved by the Commission in Opinion No.

594.” 13 In the same brief, NETOs assert that the natural break test as articulated in

Opinion No. 594 “lacks a sound financial or empirical foundation.” 14 More significantly,

several pages of Mr. McKenzie’s testimony on behalf of PTO AC are devoted to

wholesale criticism of the Commission’s policy. 15 Mr. McKenzie describes the ROE

method adopted in Opinion No. 594 as “problematic,” 16 and he asserts that “other

financial models, including the Risk Premium and Expected Earnings approaches,

continue to provide information that is relevant to an evaluation of investors’ required

cost of equity.” 17 Given this, NETOs’ assertion that PTO AC’s filing did not “advocate

for the use of novel financial models or inputs” is simply inaccurate. 18

B.       PTO AC’s Implementation of Commission Policy Is Far from Faithful

         On no fewer than 14 occasions, NETOs’ initial brief uses the word “faithful” or

“faithfully” in describing PTO AC’s implementation of Commission policy in proposing

a base ROE of 11.39 percent. 19 PTO AC, however, falls short of faithfulness in several

material respects.

          As an initial matter, the apparent premise of such claims – that implementing

Commission policy merely involves the mechanical input of current market data into a

model – is an oversimplification. As Acadia Center explains, the Commission’s ROE

method “is not a self-executing formula . . . but a framework that requires the exercise of

judgment in selecting and implementing model inputs, screening results, and weighing

competing methodologies.” 20 As Trial Staff discussed in its initial brief and further

details in the sections below, PTO AC’s judgments in this regard are, in several respects,

inconsistent with Commission policy.

         But beyond such flawed judgment calls, PTO AC made several blatant errors in its

filing, severely undermining any claims of “faithful” implementation. First, as NETOs

admit, Mr. McKenzie erroneously excluded Fortis Inc. (Fortis) from his initial proxy

group. 21 Mr. McKenzie did not make an explicit decision to exclude it; rather, he simply

failed to address it either way in his analysis. This is a significant oversight that calls into

question other aspects of PTO AC’s proposal. Although NETOs concede that Fortis

should have been in the initial proxy group, they nonetheless claim – conveniently – that

Fortis’s inclusion does not alter the conclusion that 11.39 percent is a just-and-reasonable

base ROE. 22 As demonstrated in section D.2, below, this is incorrect. The inclusion of

Fortis has a material effect on the ROE analysis.

analysis. 23

         And third, Mr. McKenzie improperly stated the market capitalization of Hydro

One Limited (Hydro One) in Canadian dollars. 24 To be clear, Hydro One should be

excluded from the proxy group for the reasons discussed in section D.3, below.

However, if the Commission were to include the company, its market capitalization

should be converted to U.S. dollars to match the currency used to derive the size

adjustment premium. 25 This is especially important given that Hydro One’s CAPM value

would determine the low end of the CAPM range, which is used to develop the midpoint

result. 26

         Bloomberg Betas Are in the Record

proceeding is consistent with both precedent and financial evidence. 27 NETOs are

          The Commission has repeatedly ruled that, where Bloomberg betas are in the

record – as they are here – Bloomberg betas should be used. 28 NETOs do not identify a

single case in which either the Commission or a court found the use of Value Line betas

to be permissible when Bloomberg betas were also available.

         In fact, the D.C. Circuit decision that NETOs cite in support of the use of Value

Line betas vividly drives home the point that their use is only proper in the context of a

limited record. There the court explained that “no party provided adjusted betas from the

appropriate time frame based on the S&P 500” and held that it was therefore “not

arbitrary and capricious for FERC to do the best it could with the data it had.” 29 In other

words, because Bloomberg betas were not available, it was permissible to use Value Line

betas. The court further noted that, in a more recent proceeding, “FERC did have access

to adjusted betas based on the S&P 500, so it used them.” 30

D.       NETOs Fail to Demonstrate that PTO AC’s Proxy Group Is Consistent with
         Commission Policy

         NETOs essentially portray Opinion No. 594’s proxy group screening criteria as

equivalent to a formula that the PTO AC simply used to plug in updated information to

create a proxy group. NETOs further argue that PTO AC precisely applied the purported

formula in Opinion No. 594 to create its proxy group and the proposed ROE. Both

assertions are incorrect.

         First, the five screening criteria set out by the Commission in Opinion No. 594

balance objective, fact-based inquiries with judgments that require discretion. In Opinion

No. 594, the Commission adopted four initial screens that do not rely on the mechanical

results of a DCF or CAPM analysis. Those four screens are: (1) the use of a national

group of companies considered electric utilities by Value Line, (2) the inclusion of

companies with credit ratings no more than one notch above or below the utility or

utilities whose ROE is at issue, (3) the inclusion of companies that pay dividends and

have neither made nor announced a dividend cut during the six-month study period that is

significant enough to distort the study inputs, and (4) the inclusion of companies with no

merger activity during the six-month study period that is significant enough to distort the

study inputs. 38

594, the Commission included Algonquin in the proxy group even though it was not

listed as an electric utility by Value Line, noting that while being listed in Value Line was

sufficient to be included in the proxy group, it was not necessary. 39 Instead, the

Commission emphasized the purpose of the screen – which it said was to “ensure that

proxy group companies share common attributes and risks with the companies whose

ROEs they inform.” 40 And further, the analysis of merger activity requires a close

examination of the impacts of that merger activity on the company as a whole – rather

than a simple per se exclusion of a company because it had some form of merger

activity. 41

         The Commission’s fifth and final screen applies threshold tests of economic logic

to both the CAPM and DCF results. While these threshold tests of economic logic

include high-end and low-end outlier tests with prescribed limitations, they also include a

natural break test, for which the Commission explicitly decided to not set a specific limit

– instead emphasizing the importance of flexibility and discretion. 42

            2. Fortis should be included in the proxy group because it passes the natural
              break test.
           In their initial brief, NETOs acknowledge that Mr. McKenzie originally erred by

excluding Fortis from inclusion in the proxy group. Yet NETOs assert that even though

Fortis passes the first four screens established by the Commission in Opinion No. 594,

the company should nevertheless be excluded from the proxy group under the natural

break test. 66 As a result, NETOs argue, even with the inclusion of Fortis in the proxy

group, the proposed ROE of 11.39% remains just and reasonable. Contrary to the

NETOs conclusion, Fortis passes the natural break test and does affect the resulting ROE.

           Opinion No. 594 sets out the terms of the natural break test to be applied to

potential proxy group companies. Specifically, the Commission explains that the natural

break analysis determines whether “certain proxy group companies screened as outliers,

or those almost screened as outliers,” should be removed from the proxy group. 67 The

Commission further explains that this analysis typically “involves examining the distance

between that proxy group company and the next closest proxy group company and

comparing that to the dispersion of other proxy group companies.” 68 Importantly, the

Commission does not explicitly define how large of a difference constitutes a natural

break. 69 In place of a rigid formula for the application of a natural break analysis, the

           Although NETOs argue that Fortis should be excluded from the proxy group

application of the natural break test as described in Opinion No. 594. In his supplemental

Because these two high values should be excluded under the natural break test, Mr.

McKenzie argues that it is logical to also exclude Fortis from the proxy group because its

basis-point break from the next highest value is comparably large. 73

proxy group. As explained above, Eversource should be included in the proxy group. If
